text: The Boeing Company, along with its subsidiaries, is one of the world’s major aerospace firms. It operates in four reportable segments: Commercial Airplanes (BCA), Defense, Space & Security (BDS), Global Services (BGS), and Boeing Capital (BCC). The Commercial Airplanes segment develops, produces, and markets commercial jet aircraft and provides fleet support services primarily to the global commercial airline industry. This segment offers a family of commercial jetliners, including the 737 narrow-body model and the 747, 767, 777, and 787 wide-body models, with ongoing development of certain 737 MAX derivatives and the 777X program. The Defense, Space & Security segment engages in the research, development, production, and modification of manned and unmanned military aircraft, weapons systems, and related services, including fighter and trainer aircraft, vertical lift platforms, and strategic defense and intelligence systems such as C4ISR, cyber solutions, and satellite systems. Its primary customer is the United States Department of Defense (U.S. DoD), which accounted for approximately 86% of its 2018 revenues, with other significant customers including NASA and international defense, civil, and commercial satellite markets. Key products include the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet, F-15 Strike Eagle, P-8 programs, KC-46A Tanker, T-X Trainer, CH-47 Chinook, AH-64 Apache, V-22 Osprey, and space and missile systems such as government and commercial satellites, the International Space Station, Commercial Crew, missile defense, and Joint Direct Attack Munition, as well as the United Launch Alliance joint venture. The Global Services segment provides a full range of services to commercial and defense customers, including supply chain and logistics, engineering, maintenance, modifications, upgrades, spare parts, pilot and maintenance training, technical documentation, and data analytics. The Boeing Capital segment ensures customers have access to financing for purchasing and delivering Boeing products and manages overall financing exposure through a portfolio of equipment under operating leases, finance leases, notes, receivables, assets held for sale or re-lease, and investments. Boeing owns numerous patents and holds licenses for third-party patents related to its products and manufacturing processes; the U.S. government has licenses for patents developed under government contracts and may use or authorize others to use such inventions for government purposes. Unpatented research, development, engineering skills, trademarks, trade secrets, and other intellectual property also contribute significantly to the business. While intellectual property rights are important, Boeing does not believe its business would be materially affected by the expiration of any particular patent or termination of any specific patent license. As of December 31, 2018, the total workforce was approximately 153,000, with principal collective bargaining agreements in place with the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (22% of employees, agreements expiring in June 2022 and September 2024), the Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace (11%, agreements expiring in October 2022), and the United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (1%, agreement expiring in October 2022). The commercial jet aircraft market and airline industry are highly competitive, with aggressive international competitors such as Airbus, Russia, China, and Japan; Boeing focuses on improving processes and reducing costs to offer greater value. The Defense, Space & Security segment faces strong competition from Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, General Dynamics, and SpaceX, with non-U.S. companies like BAE Systems and Airbus expanding their presence in the U.S. through North American operations and partnerships. BGS competes in a challenging market with many of the same U.S. and non-U.S. competitors and intends to grow market share through high customer satisfaction and productivity. Boeing’s businesses are heavily regulated, involving numerous U.S. government agencies such as the U.S. military, NASA, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), and the Department of Homeland Security, as well as similar authorities in non-U.S. markets. Government contracts may be terminated at the government’s convenience or for default; in the case of convenience termination, Boeing is generally entitled to payment for completed work and allowable termination costs, while in default termination, the government pays only for accepted work and may require Boeing to cover the cost difference between the original contract and reprocurement, net of accepted work, and may hold Boeing liable for damages. Commercial aircraft must comply with FAA regulations on production, quality, airworthiness, repair procedures, and operational safety, with similar requirements in non-U.S. markets administered by national aviation authorities or the European Joint Aviation Authorities. Boeing is subject to environmental laws and regulations regarding the discharge, treatment, storage, disposal, and remediation of hazardous substances and wastes, with environmental compliance costs being a normal, recurring part of operations and often allowable under U.S. government contracts. It is reasonably possible that additional environmental regulations or contamination discoveries could materially impact results of operations, financial condition, or cash flows. As a Potentially Responsible Party (PRP), Boeing may be jointly and severally liable for the full cost of remediating contamination at its facilities or former facilities or at third-party sites, and under the statutory framework, it may pursue contribution rights from other PRPs. Non-U.S. sales are subject to U.S. and non-U.S. regulations on import-export controls, tariffs, investment, exchange controls, anti-corruption, and repatriation of earnings, along with currency, political, and economic risks. Boeing is highly dependent on the availability of raw materials, parts, and subassemblies from suppliers and subcontractors, with key materials including aluminum, titanium, and composites; although alternatives exist, qualification can take a year or more, and many major components are procured on a sole-source basis. Boeing relies on a large number of U.S. and non-U.S. suppliers to meet performance specifications, quality standards, and delivery schedules at anticipated costs; failure by suppliers to meet commitments could disrupt production and impact profitability. The company is also dependent on affordable energy sources such as electricity. No material portion of Boeing’s business is considered seasonal. The business of Boeing is considered to be seasonal. The Commercial Airplanes and Global Services businesses depend heavily on commercial airlines and are subject to unique risks. Market conditions significantly impact demand for commercial aircraft and related services, which are primarily driven by long-term trends in airline passenger and cargo traffic, including sustained economic growth and political stability in both developed and emerging markets. Demand is also influenced by airline profitability, aircraft financing availability, world trade policies, government-to-government relations, technological advances, price and competitive factors, fuel prices, terrorism, epidemics, and environmental regulations. The airline industry is traditionally cyclical and highly competitive, with significant profit swings and ongoing challenges to achieve cost competitiveness. Financing availability for non-U.S. customers depends in part on the Export-Import Bank of the United States being fully operational. A significant deterioration in the global economic environment, the airline industry, or the financial stability of one or more major customers could result in fewer new orders, delays or cancellations of contractual orders or payments, leading to lower revenues, profitability, and cash flows, and a reduction in contractual backlog. Because the commercial aircraft backlog consists of aircraft scheduled for delivery over several years, macroeconomic, industry, or customer impacts could unexpectedly affect deliveries over a long period. Boeing enters into firm fixed-price aircraft sales contracts with indexed price escalation clauses that could subject the company to losses if cost overruns occur or if cost increases exceed the applicable escalation rate. These contracts are often entered into years before delivery, and pricing is based on a fixed amount modified by escalation formulas derived from labor, commodity, and other price indices. Revenue estimates are based on current expectations of these formulas, but actual escalation amounts are outside of Boeing’s control and can fluctuate significantly, impacting revenues and operating margins. A significant portion of Boeing’s revenues comes from a limited number of commercial airlines, and there is no assurance that any customer will exercise purchase options, fulfill existing commitments, or purchase additional products or services. Fleet decisions, airline consolidations, or financial challenges involving major customers could significantly reduce revenues and limit profit opportunities. The Commercial Airplanes business depends on maintaining a healthy production system, achieving planned production targets, successfully developing new aircraft or derivatives, and meeting or exceeding stringent performance and reliability standards. The business is extremely complex, involving extensive coordination with U.S. and non-U.S. suppliers, highly skilled labor, and stringent regulatory requirements. Introducing new aircraft programs, such as the 777X, involves increased risks related to meeting development, testing, production, and certification schedules. The ability to deliver aircraft on time, satisfy regulatory and customer requirements, and achieve program profitability is subject to significant risks. Boeing must minimize disruption from production changes and achieve productivity improvements to meet customer demand and maintain profitability. The company has plans to adjust production rates on several commercial aircraft programs while continuing significant development and production of the 777X. It also seeks to reduce aircraft-building costs by working with suppliers to reduce costs, identifying and implementing productivity improvements, and optimizing inventory management. Delays or significant disruptions in production rate changes at commercial aircraft assembly facilities, or if suppliers cannot deliver components at the required cost and rates, could prevent the company from meeting delivery schedules or negatively affect financial performance. Operational challenges, such as delays or defects in supplier components, failure to meet internal performance plans, or delays in achieving required regulatory certifications, could result in out-of-sequence work, increased production costs, delayed deliveries, impacts to aircraft performance, and higher warranty or fleet support costs. If Boeing’s commercial airplanes fail to meet performance or reliability requirements, the company could face additional costs and/or lower revenues. Developing and manufacturing aircraft that meet or exceed performance and reliability standards, as well as those of customers and regulatory agencies, is costly and technologically challenging, especially with newer programs. Any failure of a Boeing aircraft to meet these requirements could disrupt operations, increase costs, and reduce revenues. Revenue from the U.S. government, primarily from defense-related programs with the U.S. Department of Defense (U.S. DoD), constitutes a substantial portion of Boeing’s revenue. U.S. defense spending is difficult to predict and may be affected by political environment, foreign policy, macroeconomic conditions, and the ability of the U.S. government to pass authorization and appropriations bills. The Bipartisan Budget Act of 2018 raised preexisting spending caps for fiscal years 2018 and 2019 (FY18 and FY19). Consolidated spending bills signed in September 2018 provided defense funding for FY19, but other departments, including NASA and the FAA, were temporarily funded at FY18 levels. Failure to enact a Continuing Resolution or FY19 appropriations by February 15, 2019, would result in a partial government shutdown affecting these agencies, which could impact Boeing’s operations. Reduced discretionary spending limits enacted in 2011 would take effect again in fiscal years 2020 and 2021 (FY20 and FY21) unless Congress acts to raise spending caps or repeal or suspend the law. Continued budget uncertainty and the risk of future sequestration cuts remain, and U.S. government discretionary spending levels are likely to face ongoing pressure. There is significant uncertainty regarding future program-level appropriations for the U.S. DoD and other agencies, including NASA. While the House and Senate Appropriations Committees included funding for Boeing’s major programs—such as the F/A-18 Super Hornet, CH-47 Chinook, AH-64 Apache, V-22 Osprey, KC-46A Pegasus Tanker, and P-8 Poseidon—in their final FY19 defense appropriations, uncertainty remains about how defense budgets in FY20 and beyond will affect Boeing’s programs. Future budget cuts or changes in investment priorities, including those related to authorizations and appropriations, could result in reductions, cancellations, or delays of existing contracts or programs, which could materially affect the company’s operations, financial position, and cash flows. Due to ongoing uncertainty about U.S. defense spending levels and the threat environment, the U.S. DoD is expected to continue emphasizing cost-cutting and efficiency initiatives in procurement. If Boeing cannot successfully adapt to these changing acquisition priorities or fails to meet affordability targets set by the U.S. DoD, its revenues and market share would be further impacted. A significant portion of Boeing’s business is conducted pursuant to U.S. government contracts, which are subject to unique risks. In 2018, 31% of Boeing’s revenues were earned from U.S. government contracts, including foreign military sales (FMS) through the U.S. government. These contracts are subject to extensive procurement regulations and other unique risks. Sales to the U.S. government are subject to extensive procurement regulations, and changes to these regulations could increase compliance costs. New regulations or changes to existing requirements could increase compliance costs or otherwise materially impact the operating margins of Boeing’s BDS and BGS businesses. These requirements may result in increased compliance costs and could lead to withheld payments or reduced future business if Boeing fails to comply. The U.S. government may modify, curtail, or terminate one or more of Boeing’s contracts without prior notice, either at its convenience or for default based on performance. Funding under U.S. government contracts may be reduced or withheld due to fiscal constraints, changes in national security strategy or priorities, or other reasons. Uncertainty about ongoing programs could also arise if the U.S. government finances operations through temporary measures like “continuing resolutions” instead of full-year appropriations. Any loss or anticipated loss of funding, or modification, curtailment, or termination of large programs, could have a material adverse effect on earnings, cash flow, and financial position. Boeing is subject to U.S. government inquiries and investigations, including periodic audits of costs deemed reimbursable under government contracts. Agencies such as the Defense Contract Audit Agency and the Defense Contract Management Agency routinely audit contractors, reviewing performance, cost structure, compliance with laws and regulations, internal control systems, and policies. Costs found to be misclassified or inaccurately allocated to a specific contract are deemed non-reimbursable, and any already reimbursed amounts must be refunded. Inadequacies in systems and policies could result in withholds on billed receivables, penalties, and reduced future business. If an audit, inquiry, or investigation uncovers improper or illegal activities, Boeing could face civil and criminal penalties, administrative sanctions, including contract termination, forfeiture of profits, suspension of payments, fines, and suspension or debarment from doing business with the U.S. government. The company could also suffer reputational harm if allegations of impropriety are made, even if later found to be false. Boeing enters into fixed-price contracts that could subject it to losses if cost overruns occur. The BDS and BGS defense businesses generated approximately 65% and 77% of their 2018 revenues from fixed-price contracts. While fixed-price contracts allow benefits from performance improvements and cost reductions, they also expose the company to reduced margins or losses if estimated costs exceed estimated revenues. If estimated costs exceed estimated prices, Boeing recognizes reach-forward losses, which can significantly affect reported results. For example, in 2018, Boeing recorded reach-forward losses totaling $736 million on the USAF KC-46A Tanker contract, primarily due to higher estimated costs related to certification, testing, and change incorporation, as well as higher-than-expected effort to meet customer requirements for initial aircraft delivery. In addition, in 2018, Boeing recorded a $400 million loss related to options for 346 T-X Trainer aircraft and a $291 million loss related to the MQ-25 Stingray Engineering, Manufacturing and Development (EMD) contract in connection with winning those competitions. The long-term nature of many contracts makes cost and revenue estimation inherently risky. Fixed-price contracts often include performance-based price incentives and penalties that are difficult to estimate and have significant impacts on margins. Some contracts contain specific provisions related to cost, schedule, and performance. Fixed-price development contracts are generally more uncertain than production contracts, as many involve highly complex designs. Technical or quality issues during development can lead to schedule delays and higher completion costs, resulting in material charges or adverse financial impacts. Significant BDS fixed-price development contracts include Commercial Crew, Saudi F-15, USAF KC-46A Tanker, T-X Trainer, VC-25B Presidential Aircraft, MQ-25 Stingray, and commercial and military satellites. Boeing also enters into cost-type contracts, which carry risks. The BDS and BGS defense businesses generated approximately 35% and 23% of their 2018 revenues from cost-type contracting arrangements. Some of these are development programs with complex design and technical challenges. These cost-type programs typically have award or incentive fees that are uncertain and may be earned over extended periods. Financial risks are primarily related to reduced fees, lower profit rates, or program cancellation if cost, schedule, or technical performance issues arise. Programs with primarily cost-type contracts include GMD, Proprietary, and SLS programs. Boeing also enters into contracts that include in-orbit incentive payments, which subject the company to risks. Contracts in the commercial satellite industry and certain government satellite contracts include in-orbit incentive payments, which may be paid over time after final satellite acceptance or paid in full prior to acceptance. In both cases, the incentive payment is at risk if the satellite fails to perform to specifications for up to 15 years after acceptance. The net present value of in-orbit incentive fees is recognized as revenue during the construction period. If the satellite fails to meet contractual performance criteria, customers will not be obligated to make in-orbit payments, and Boeing may be required to provide refunds, incurring significant charges. Boeing’s ability to deliver products and services that meet customer requirements is heavily dependent on the performance and financial stability of its subcontractors and suppliers, as well as the availability of raw materials and components. The company relies on U.S. and non-U.S. subcontractors and suppliers to provide raw materials, integrated components, sub-assemblies, and production commodities, and to perform certain services. If one or more suppliers or subcontractors experience financial difficulties, delivery delays, or performance problems, Boeing may be unable to meet customer commitments or incur additional costs. For example, the 737 program experienced supply chain disruptions in 2018 that affected delivery timing. If raw materials on which Boeing depends—such as aluminum, titanium, or composites—become unavailable or are available only at very high prices, the company may be unable to deliver products in a timely manner or at budgeted costs. In some instances, Boeing depends on a single source of supply. Any service disruption from one such source could have significant consequences.

Our ability to deliver products and services that meet customer requirements is heavily dependent on the financial stability and performance of our subcontractors and suppliers, as well as the availability of raw materials and components. We rely on U.S. and non-U.S. subcontractors and suppliers to provide raw materials, integrated components, sub-assemblies, production commodities, and certain services. If any supplier or subcontractor faces financial difficulties, delivery delays, or performance issues, we may fail to meet customer commitments or incur additional costs. For example, the 737 program experienced supply chain disruptions in 2018 that affected delivery timing. If key raw materials such as aluminum, titanium, or composites become unavailable or are only available at very high prices, we may be unable to deliver products on time or at budgeted costs. In some cases, we depend on a single source of supply, and disruptions—whether due to geopolitical events, performance problems, or financial instability—could materially harm our ability to meet customer commitments or increase operating costs. We use estimates in contract and program accounting, which involves judgment in assessing risks, estimating revenues and costs, and making assumptions about schedules, technical issues, and performance. Due to the size and complexity of many contracts, estimating total revenues and costs at completion is difficult and subject to numerous variables, including expected wage and benefit increases, material price fluctuations, allocated fixed costs, and changes in price escalation indices. Incentives and penalties are considered in sales and profit rate estimates when sufficient information is available, and supplier assertions are also evaluated. For commercial aircraft programs, inventoriable production costs, program tooling, non-recurring costs, and routine warranty costs are accumulated and charged to cost of sales by program rather than by individual units or contracts. A program is defined by an estimated number of units to be produced in a long-term effort under existing and anticipated contracts, limited by the ability to make reliable estimates. Key factors influencing the accounting quantity include firm orders, letters of intent, market studies, and changes in customer or model mix, production costs, learning curves, supplier performance, negotiations, and certification issues. Any changes in these estimates could negatively affect future financial performance. Because of the significant judgment and estimation involved, materially different sales and profit figures could result from different assumptions or changing circumstances, which may adversely affect future financial results. Competition in our markets, particularly in commercial airplanes and defense sectors, is intense, with competitors having more advanced engineering, manufacturing, or marketing capabilities. In commercial aviation, non-U.S. manufacturers are expected to increase competition, and in BDS, defense industry consolidation, reduced program volume, and cost competitiveness pressures will intensify competition. Our BGS segment faces similar competition as BCA and BDS. We also face growing international competition and cross-border consolidation. There is no guarantee we will successfully compete, and competitive pressures could reduce revenues and market share. A significant portion of our revenues—approximately 56% in 2018—comes from non-U.S. customers, including FMS, and we expect this to remain a major source of revenue. As a result, we face international risks such as changes in regulatory requirements, government policies (including local funding requirements and industrial participation), currency exchange rate fluctuations, political and economic volatility, complexity of managing non-U.S. representatives, financing uncertainties, funding restrictions, taxes, export controls, tariffs, embargoes, sanctions, operational challenges across multiple countries, compliance with various laws, and unforeseen events like terrorism, war, epidemics, or conflicts. While the impact is hard to predict, any of these factors could harm our operations. Unauthorized access to our or our customers’ information systems could damage our business, leading to financial or reputational harm. We maintain extensive technical security controls, policies, monitoring, and oversight to prevent, detect, and respond to threats, but cyber-attacks could still result in significant losses. We also manage information systems for customers who face similar risks; if we fail to protect their confidential, classified, or personally identifiable data, our reputation could suffer and we could face financial losses. Litigation and government inquiries are unpredictable, and an adverse outcome could materially affect our financial position and operations. We are involved in multiple litigation matters that may divert financial and management resources, and no assurance exists that outcomes will be favorable. Government investigations, due to our relationships with the U.S. government, industry regulation, or environmental issues, could lead to adverse rulings. A significant portion of our customer financing portfolio is concentrated among certain customers and in specific aircraft types, such as the 717 and 747-8, and among customers with below-investment-grade credit. If one or more of these customers defaults or fails to renew leases, and we cannot redeploy the aircraft on reasonable terms, or if the concentrated aircraft types experience value declines, our earnings, cash flows, and financial position could be materially harmed. We may not be able to obtain debt at competitive rates, on commercially reasonable terms, or in sufficient amounts to fund operations and commitments. As of December 31, 2018, our airplane financing commitments totaled $19,462 million, up from $10,221 million in 2017. Disruptions in global capital markets or declines in our financial performance or credit ratings could increase borrowing costs and reduce access to public and private debt markets, negatively affecting our ability to meet obligations. Mergers, acquisitions, joint ventures, or divestitures may not yield expected benefits due to integration challenges, underperformance of products or management, legacy liabilities, transaction costs, amortization of intangibles, asset impairments, credit guarantees, partner performance, or indemnifications. Consolidations in joint ventures could also affect reported results. While we have established procedures to mitigate these risks, there is no assurance of success. Divestitures may result in continued financial involvement through guarantees or other arrangements, and nonperformance by divested businesses could lead to additional payments, higher costs, or asset write-downs. Our insurance coverage may not be sufficient to cover all significant risks, especially for products like aircraft technologies, missile systems, border security systems, anti-terrorism technologies, and air traffic management systems, which may not be insurable on commercially reasonable terms. While some of these products are protected under the SAFETY Act in the U.S., such protection does not extend abroad, potentially resulting in significant liabilities. The amount of insurance we maintain may be inadequate to cover these or other claims. Business disruptions from threats to physical security, information technology, cyber-attacks, natural disasters, or pandemics could seriously affect sales, financial condition, and increase costs. Significant production delays or damage to data, systems, or networks could impact sales, increase expenses, and harm Boeing’s reputation. Approximately 54,000 employees, or 35% of our total workforce as of December 31, 2018, were union-represented. We experienced a work stoppage in 2008 that halted commercial aircraft and certain BDS production, and future stoppages are possible. We cannot predict the stability of our relationships with 11 U.S. and 13 non-U.S. labor organizations or whether we can meet union demands without impacting our financial condition. Union actions at suppliers can also affect us, and work stoppages or instability could delay product development and production, strain customer relationships, and reduce revenues. We have substantial pension and postretirement benefit obligations, primarily under defined benefit pension plans. Future contributions depend on market factors such as discount rates and actual returns on plan assets. Changes in these assumptions can significantly affect future contributions and annual pension costs, as well as shareholders’ equity. For U.S. government contracts, pension costs are allocated based on U.S. Cost Accounting Standards, which can impact contract profitability. We also provide health care benefits to retirees and qualifying dependents, with future costs based on medical cost estimates. These estimates are subject to assumptions, and changes could affect financial statements. Although GAAP does not directly link pension expenses to cash contributions, key economic factors affecting GAAP expenses also influence cash or stock contributions. We are exposed to material environmental liabilities under U.S. and non-U.S. environmental laws, including those related to hazardous substances and waste. We could face substantial costs, including cleanup, fines, civil or criminal penalties, and third-party claims for property damage or personal injury, due to violations or liabilities from current or past operations or acquired companies. Indemnification agreements with third parties may also expose us to such costs. New laws, stricter enforcement, discovery of unknown contamination, or new remediation requirements could lead to additional expenses. The company's principal operations are in the U.S., but it conducts operations in an expanding number of countries and relies on an extensive network of non-U.S. partners, key suppliers, and subcontractors. Its strategy centers on successful execution in its core businesses—Commercial Airplanes (BCA), Defense, Space & Security (BDS), and Global Services (BGS)—supplemented by Boeing Capital (BCC). These core businesses have historically generated substantial earnings and cash flow, enabling investment in new products and services. BCA is committed to being the leader in commercial aviation by offering airplanes and services that deliver superior design, efficiency, and value to customers worldwide. BDS integrates its resources in defense, intelligence, communications, security, space, and services to deliver capability-driven solutions at reduced costs, with a strategy to leverage core businesses to capture key next-generation programs and expand in adjacent and international markets. BGS provides support for commercial and defense through innovative, comprehensive, and cost-competitive product and service solutions. BCC facilitates, arranges, structures, and provides selective financing solutions for Boeing customers. Revenues for the year ended December 31, 2018, were $101,127 million, an 8% increase from $94,005 million in 2017, driven by higher revenues at BCA, BDS, and BGS. BCA revenues increased by $2,701 million due to higher 737 and 787 deliveries and a favorable model mix, which more than offset lower 777 and 747 deliveries. BDS revenues increased by $2,634 million primarily due to non-U.S. contract awards for fighters, higher weapons revenue, the final C-17 aircraft sale, and higher satellite revenue. BGS revenues increased by $2,437 million due to growth across its services portfolio, primarily driven by higher parts revenue including the acquisition of KLX Inc. (KLX). These increases were partially offset by lower unallocated revenue. Revenues in 2017 increased by $509 million or 1% compared to 2016, with BDS revenues rising $381 million due to higher weapons revenue and BGS revenues increasing $762 million due to higher commercial parts revenue. These gains were partially offset by lower BCA revenues, primarily due to delivery mix, with fewer twin-aisle deliveries more than offsetting the impact of higher single-aisle deliveries. Changes in unallocated items, eliminations, and other in 2018, 2017, and 2016 primarily reflect the timing of eliminations for intercompany aircraft deliveries and the sale of aircraft previously leased to customers. Earnings from operations for 2018 were $11,987 million, an increase of $1,643 million from 2017, primarily due to higher earnings at BCA and BGS, which more than offset the decrease at BDS and the change in unallocated items, eliminations, and other. BCA earnings from operations increased by $2,427 million due to higher revenues and improved operating margins, driven by higher 787 margins, improved cost performance, and favorable delivery mix. BGS earnings from operations increased by $276 million due to higher revenues, partially offset by higher period costs. BDS earnings from operations decreased by $599 million in 2018 compared to 2017 as revenue growth was more than offset by charges of $691 million related to winning the T-X Trainer and MQ-25 competitions and $199 million of higher KC-46A Tanker reach-forward losses. Earnings from operations in 2017 increased by $3,817 million compared to 2016 due to higher earnings at BCA and BDS, partially offset by changes in unallocated items, eliminations, and other. Program accounting requires the demonstrated ability to reliably estimate the relationship of sales to costs for the defined program accounting quantity. A program consists of the estimated number of units (accounting quantity) of a product to be produced in a continuing, long-term production effort for delivery under existing and anticipated contracts. The determination of the accounting quantity is limited by the ability to make reasonably dependable estimates of the revenue and cost of existing and anticipated contracts. For each program, the amount reported as cost of sales is determined by applying the estimated cost of sales percentage for the total remaining program to the amount of sales recognized for airplanes delivered and accepted by the customer. Factors that must be estimated include program accounting quantity, sales price, labor and employee benefit costs, material costs, procured part costs, major component costs, overhead costs, program tooling and other non-recurring costs, and warranty costs. Estimation of the accounting quantity for each program takes into account several factors that are indicative of the demand for the particular program, such as firm orders, letters of intent from prospective customers, and market studies. Total estimated program sales are determined by estimating the model mix and sales price for all unsold units within the accounting quantity, added together with the sales prices for all undelivered units under contract. The sales prices for all undelivered units within the accounting quantity include an escalation adjustment for inflation that is updated quarterly. Cost estimates are based largely on negotiated and anticipated contracts with suppliers, historical performance trends, and business base and other economic projections. Factors that influence these estimates include production rates, internal and subcontractor performance trends, customer and/or supplier claims or assertions, asset utilization, anticipated labor agreements, and inflationary or deflationary trends. Changes in estimates are normally recognized on a prospective basis; however, when estimated costs to complete a program exceed estimated revenues from undelivered units in the accounting quantity, a loss provision is recorded in the current period for the estimated loss on all undelivered units in the accounting quantity. Investment income and loss are classified on the Consolidated Statements of Operations as operating or non-operating: operating investments, which are strategically aligned with the company’s operations, include earnings from equity method investments, dividend income from other equity investments, and impairments or gains/losses on disposition, and are reported in Income from operating investments, net; non-operating investments, held for non-strategic purposes, include interest and dividends on marketable securities and related impairments or gains/losses, reported in Other income/(loss), net. All derivative instruments are recognized and measured at fair value regardless of purpose. For fair value hedges, gains or losses are recognized in earnings along with the offsetting gain or loss on the hedged item, with the ineffective portion of the hedge recognized in earnings. For cash flow hedges, the effective portion is initially recorded in comprehensive income and reclassified to earnings when the hedged forecasted transaction affects earnings; the ineffective portion is recognized in earnings immediately. Aluminum purchase and sale agreements, used to meet long-term strategic sourcing and international business needs, are derivatives but are not designated for hedge accounting; changes in their fair value are recorded in earnings immediately. Used aircraft under trade-in commitments and repurchase commitments are managed through agreements with customers: trade-in commitments allow customers to trade in used aircraft at a specified price upon purchase of new aircraft, and repurchase commitments obligate the company to repurchase new aircraft 10 to 15 years after delivery, contingent on a future agreement to sell additional new aircraft. If a new aircraft sale agreement is executed and the customer exercises the right to sell the aircraft, a contingent repurchase commitment becomes a trade-in commitment. Historical experience shows such conversions are infrequent. Exposure from trade-in commitments may include adjustments to revenue for the difference between the contractual trade-in price and the best estimate of fair value of the aircraft at the time of the agreement, recognized upon delivery, or charges to cost of products for adverse changes in fair value prior to purchase, with estimates included in Accrued liabilities. Fair value of trade-in aircraft is determined using model, age, condition, market conditions, and multiple valuation sources, with valuation based on market opportunities such as resale, leasing (with possible refurbishment costs), or scrap. Valuations are updated quarterly based on actual market activities or third-party valuations adjusted for individual attributes. Used aircraft acquired by the Commercial Airplanes segment are included in Inventories at the lower of cost or net realizable value, and may be placed on operating lease, during which time they are included in Customer financing. Customer financing includes operating lease equipment, notes receivable, and sales-type/finance leases, with sales-type/finance leases treated as receivables and allowances for losses established as needed. The fair value of assets, including equipment under operating leases, assets held for sale or re-lease, and collateral underlying receivables, is assessed to determine if fair value is less than carrying value; differences for sales-type/finance leases and notes receivables are considered in determining the allowance for losses. Fair value of aircraft is determined using a median from published third-party aircraft value publications based on type and age, with judgment applied when specific aircraft features differ significantly from standard models. Impairment reviews for assets under operating leases or held for sale or re-lease occur when events or changes indicate expected undiscounted cash flows may be less than carrying value, using assumptions such as lease term, future lease rates, residual value, remarketing costs, maintenance, and economic life. Assets held for sale are recorded at the lower of carrying value or fair value less costs to sell. When impairment is indicated, the expense is the excess of carrying value over fair value. The allowance for losses on customer financing receivables is a valuation account reflecting probable but unconfirmed losses, including receivables evaluated individually and all other receivables. A receivable is considered impaired if it is probable the company will not collect amounts due under the original terms, without restructuring, based on factors such as extended delinquency or bankruptcy filings. The specific impairment allowance is based on the difference between carrying value and estimated fair value of related collateral. The allowance for remaining receivables is reviewed by assessing collateral exposure (the excess of carrying value over fair value of collateral) and cumulative default rate, which is derived from customer credit ratings and weighted average remaining contract term. Internally assigned credit ratings are updated based on public information and direct customer data. Agreements with certain customers allow the company to look beyond specific collateral in a default situation, enabling the sale or retention of other customer assets to cover shortfalls. Each quarter, the company reviews customer credit ratings, historical default rates, and third-party aircraft valuations to validate the allowance for losses. There is no assurance actual results will match estimates or that future considerations will not alter the allowance. Warranties provided with product sales, primarily by the Commercial Airplanes segment, cover non-conformance and defects in material or design. Most aircraft sales include a 3 to 4-year standard warranty for systems, accessories, equipment, parts, and software, included in the program’s estimate at completion. Occasionally, commitments beyond standard warranties are made to address fleet-wide major issues, resulting in additional accrued warranty expenses. Warranties from the BDS segment, related to military aircraft and weapons hardware, cover systems, accessories, equipment, parts, and software under contractual specifications and typically last from six months to two years, included in contract cost estimates. Estimated costs for standard warranties are recorded when the product is delivered. The warranty liability at each balance sheet date reflects the estimated number of months of warranty coverage outstanding multiplied by the average of historical monthly payments, plus additional amounts for major warranty issues exceeding normal claim levels, with changes to the initial estimate recorded as adjustments. Performance guarantees to commercial airplane customers, including compensation for failure to meet performance targets, are accounted for as warranties. The estimated liability is based on operational characteristics, forecasted customer use, and anticipated settlements, and is recorded as a reduction of revenue at delivery. Agreements with suppliers that require them to compensate the company for customer claims due to failure of supplied equipment to meet performance targets are included in Inventories and recorded as a reduction in Cost of products at delivery. These performance warranties and supplier claims are included in the programs’ estimate at completion. Supplier penalties are accrued when an event makes it probable a penalty will be incurred and the amount is reasonably estimable; until such an event, the company fully anticipates accepting all products under production-related contracts. Guarantees issued or modified after December 31, 2002, are recorded in Accrued liabilities at fair value; for credit guarantees, the liability equals the present value of expected loss, calculated by multiplying the creditor’s default rate by the guarantee amount reduced by expected recovery for each future period. If at inception a probable contingent loss exists, a liability is recognized for the greater of (a) the fair value of the guarantee or (b) the probable contingent loss.
